title: حِكَايَةُ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ مَعَ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
titleEn: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār
part: Night 161 · ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 785–789 (Night 161, continuing directly from nights-160), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 161 continues the tale of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār. Walking home, the jeweller finds a letter lying in the road: Shams al-Nahār's, written to ʿAlī, with two lines of verse, asking why the letters between them have stopped. The slave-girl who dropped it follows him home; he makes her swear to tell him everything, tells her in turn what he knows from ʿAlī, and the two agree that she will carry the letters through him. ʿAlī answers in verse and rhymed prose, protesting his faithfulness. Next morning the girl returns: her mistress wants to hear the jeweller herself and bind him to the pledges. He is terrified of entering the caliph's palace, so the girl brings Shams al-Nahār to his house instead. She unveils, questions him about his household and about Abū al-Ḥasan's departure, and begins to speak of how nothing is gained without effort. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْحَادِيَةُ وَالسِّتُّونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-ḥādiyatu wa-al-sittūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the first-and-sixty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and sixty-first night,
sentences.n: The number is built from the inside out: al-ḥādiya, “the first”, the ordinal used for “one” inside a compound number and feminine to agree with layla; then wa-al-sittūn, “and the sixty”, which keeps its cardinal form; then baʿda al-miʾa, “after the hundred”. So the unit comes first, then the ten, then the hundred: “the first and the sixty after the hundred”. Last night's heading needed a different device (al-mūfiya li-al-sittīn, “the one completing the sixty”) because a round sixty has no ordinal; with a unit in front, the plain pattern returns. The alif of المائة is silent: the word is miʾa.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْجَوْهَرِيَّ وَدَّعَهُ وَانْصَرَفَ وَهُوَ لَا يَدْرِي كَيْفَ يَعْمَلُ فِي إِسْعَافِ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-jawhariyya waddaʿahu wa-inṣarafa wa-huwa lā yadrī kayfa yaʿmalu fī isʿāfi ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the jeweller bade-him-farewell and went-away, and he does-not know how he-should-act in the helping of ʿAlī son of Bakkār.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the jeweller took his leave of ʿAlī and went away, not knowing what he could do to help him.
sentences.n: waddaʿa, “to bid farewell to” (Form II); the shadda of ودّعه is the print's own. wa-huwa lā yadrī, “while he does not know”, is a circumstantial clause. kayfa yaʿmalu, “how he should act”: the imperfect after kayfa often carries “should”. isʿāf, “helping, granting someone what he needs” (verbal noun of Form IV asʿafa).

sentences.t: وَمَا زَالَ مَاشِيًا وَهُوَ مُتَفَكِّرٌ فِي أَمْرِهِ إِذْ رَأَى وَرَقَةً مَطْرُوحَةً فِى الطَّرِيقِ فَأَخَذَهَا وَنَظَرَ عُنْوَانَهَا وَقَرَأَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-mā zāla māshiyan wa-huwa mutafakkirun fī amrihi idh raʾā waraqatan maṭrūḥatan fī al-ṭarīqi fa-akhadhahā wa-naẓara ʿunwānahā wa-qaraʾahu
sentences.l: And he did-not cease walking, he (being) pondering on his-affair, when he-saw a paper thrown-down in the road; and he-took-it and looked-at its-address and read-it.
sentences.i: He went on walking, turning the matter over in his mind, when he saw a letter lying in the road. He picked it up, looked at the direction written on it, and read it.
sentences.n: mā zāla, “did not cease”, with an accusative (māshiyan) means “kept on walking”. idh, “when (suddenly)”, breaks into the ongoing scene. waraqa, “leaf, sheet of paper”, is the letter itself. maṭrūḥa, “thrown down, lying”, the passive participle of ṭaraḥa. ʿunwān is the superscription or direction on a folded letter, saying from whom and to whom; qaraʾahu, “he read it”, has the masculine pronoun for ʿunwān. naẓara here takes its object directly, without ilā. The shadda of متفكّر and the hamza of رأى and قرأه are the print's own; فى is its spelling of fī.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا هُوَ مِنَ الْمُحِبِّ الْأَصْغَرِ إِلَي الْحَبِيبِ الْأَكْبَرِ
sentences.tr: fa-idhā huwa mina al-muḥibbi al-aṣghari ilā al-ḥabībi al-akbari
sentences.l: And behold, it (was) from the lover, the lesser, to the beloved, the greater.
sentences.i: And there it was: “From the humbler lover to the greater beloved.”
sentences.n: fa-idhā, “and behold”, introduces what he finds. al-muḥibb, “the one who loves”, is the active participle of Form IV aḥabba; al-ḥabīb, “the beloved”. The writer calls herself “the lesser” and her beloved “the greater”, a lover's courtesy, and keeps both names out of it. The print spells ilā with a dotted yāʾ (الي), as it often does.

sentences.t: فَفَتَحَ الْوَرَقَةَ فَرَأَى مَكْتُوبًا فِيهَا هَذَانِ الْبَيْتَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-fataḥa al-waraqata fa-raʾā maktūban fīhā hādhāni al-baytāni
sentences.l: And he-opened the paper and saw written in-it these two verses:
sentences.i: He opened the letter and saw these two lines of verse written in it:
sentences.n: raʾā maktūban fīhā hādhāni al-baytāni, “he saw, written in it, these two verses”: maktūban, “written”, is what he saw, in the accusative, and hādhāni al-baytāni stands in the nominative as the subject of that participle. Compare ʿAlī's reply further on, where the same idea is put the other way round. hādhāni is the dual of hādhā; bayt, “house”, is also a line of verse.

sentences.t:
جَاءَ الرَّسُوْلُ بِوَصْلٍ مِنْكَ يَطْمَعُنِيْ * وَكَانَ اَكْثَرُ ظَنّيْ اَنَّهُ وَهَمَا
فَمَا فَرِحْتُ وَلٰكِنْ زَادَنِيْ حُزُنًا * عِلْمِيْ بِاَنَّ رَسُوْلِيْ لَمْ يَكُنْ فَهِمَا
sentences.tr:
jāʾa al-rasūlu bi-waṣlin minka yaṭmaʿunī * wa-kāna aktharu ẓannī annahu wahamā
fa-mā fariḥtu wa-lākin zādanī ḥuzunan * ʿilmī bi-anna rasūlī lam yakun fahimā
sentences.l:
The messenger came with union from-you, (a promise) making-me-hope; * and most of my-belief was that it (was) a delusion;
and I-did-not rejoice, but it-increased-me (in) grief, * my-knowing that my-messenger had not understood.
sentences.i:
The messenger brought word of a meeting with you, and it set me hoping, though most of me believed it a delusion;
so I took no joy in it; instead it only added to my grief to know that my messenger had not understood.
sentences.n: Metre: basīṭ. The pointing is the print's own, kept as printed, including the bare alif of اَكْثَرُ and اَنَّهُ where the edition marks no hamza, and the sukūn it sets on long vowels. jāʾa bi-, “to come with, bring”: bi- marks what the messenger brought; waṣl, “joining”, is a lovers' meeting. The print points يَطْمَعُنِيْ as yaṭmaʿunī, the simple verb “to covet”, which does not take an object; the sense wants the causative yuṭmiʿunī (Form IV aṭmaʿa), “making me hope”, and the translation follows that. wahamā is wahm, “delusion, fancy”, given a second vowel for the metre, with the rhyme's long -ā; likewise ḥuzunan for ḥuzn, “grief”, and the rhyme vowel of fahimā. zāda, “to increase”, takes the person and then what is added, both as objects: “it increased me in grief”. ʿilmī bi-anna …, “my knowing that …”, is the subject of zādanī; ʿalima bi-, “to know of”. lam yakun fahimā, kāna with a perfect: “had not understood”. The verses are Shams al-Nahār's, written to ʿAlī: her complaint is that her own messenger has failed her.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدُ فَاعْلَمْ يَا سَيِّدِي أَنَّنِي لَمْ أَدْرِ سَبَبَ قَطْعِ الْمُرَاسَلَةِ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿdu fa-iʿlam yā sayyidī annanī lam adri sababa qaṭʿi al-murāsalati baynī wa-baynaka
sentences.l: And after: know, O my-master, that I did-not know the cause of the cutting of the exchanging-of-letters between-me and-between-you.
sentences.i: To proceed: know, my lord, that I cannot tell why the letters between us have stopped.
sentences.n: wa-baʿdu, “and after (that)”, is the letter-writer's formula that ends the greetings and opens the business; baʿdu takes ḍamma because what it is “after” is left unsaid, and fa- follows it. sayyidī, “my master”, is the lover's address; the shadda is the print's own, as is that of انّني. lam adri: lam with the jussive of darā, “to know”, which loses its final vowel. murāsala (Form III), “sending letters to one another”, correspondence. Arabic says “between me and between you”, repeating bayna.

sentences.t: فَإِنْ يَكُنْ صَدَرَ مِنْكَ الْجَفَاءُ فَأَنَا أُقَابِلُهُ بِالْوَفَاءِ وَإِنْ يَكُنْ ذَهَبَ مِنْكَ الْوِدَادُ فَأَنَا أَحْفَظُ الْوُدَّ عَلَى الْبِعَادِ
sentences.tr: fa-in yakun ṣadara minka al-jafāʾu fa-anā uqābiluhu bi-al-wafāʾi wa-in yakun dhahaba minka al-widādu fa-anā aḥfaẓu al-wudda ʿalā al-biʿādi
sentences.l: And if it-be (that) there-has-issued from-you the coldness, then I meet-it with the faithfulness; and if it-be (that) there-has-gone from-you the affection, then I keep the love despite the distance.
sentences.i: If unkindness has come from your side, I answer it with faithfulness; and if your affection has gone, I keep my love for you, however far apart we are.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: jafāʾ / wafāʾ, then widād / biʿād. in yakun ṣadara, “if it be that … has issued”: yakun (jussive of kāna) with a perfect puts the condition in the past. ṣadara min, “to come forth from, be done by”. jafāʾ, “harshness, estrangement”, is the opposite of wafāʾ, “keeping faith”. qābala bi- (Form III), “to meet (something) with”: bi- marks what it is met with. widād and wudd both mean “love, affection”; ʿalā here is “in spite of”. The hamza of الجفاء and الوفاء is the print's own; the shadda of الودّ also.

sentences.t: فَأَنَا مَعَكَ كَمَا قَالَ الشَّاعِرُ
sentences.tr: fa-anā maʿaka kamā qāla al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: So I (am) with-you as the poet said:
sentences.i: With you I am as the poet said:

sentences.t: تِهْ اَحْتَمِلْ وَاسْتَطلْ اَصْبِرْ وَعَزَّ أهُنْ * وَوَلِّ اَقْبَلْ وَقُلْ اَسْمَعْ وَمُرْ اُطِعِ
sentences.tr: tih aḥtamil wa-istaṭil aṣbir wa-ʿazza ahun * wa-walli aqbal wa-qul asmaʿ wa-mur uṭiʿi
sentences.l: Be-haughty, I-bear (it); and be-overbearing, I-endure; and be-mighty, I-am-humbled; * and turn-away, I-come-forward; and speak, I-listen; and command, I-obey.
sentences.i: Be proud, and I will bear it; domineer, and I will be patient; be mighty, and I will be lowly; turn away, and I will come to you; speak, and I will listen; command, and I will obey.
sentences.n: Metre: basīṭ. The pointing is the print's own, kept as printed: the bare alif of the first-person verbs, the precomposed hamza of أهُنْ, and the unvowelled ṭāʾ of وَاسْتَطلْ (istaṭil). The line is six pairs, each an imperative followed by a jussive: in Arabic an imperative can stand for a condition, and the jussive gives its answer, “(if you) be proud, I bear it”. tih is the imperative of tāha, “to be haughty”; istaṭil, of Form X istaṭāla, “to lord it over”; ʿazza, “be mighty, be dear”, against ahun, from hāna, “to be lowly”; walli, Form II wallā, “to turn one's back”. The print's aqbal is pointed as from qabila, “I accept (it)”; the contrast with “turn away” suggests uqbil, “I come forward” (Form IV aqbala), which the translation follows, though either sense works. uṭiʿi, “I obey” (Form IV aṭāʿa), takes a kasra for the rhyme.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا قَرَأَهَا وَإِذَا بِالْجَارِيَةِ أَقْبَلَتْ وَهِيَ تَلْتَفِتُ يَمِينًا وَشِمَالًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā qaraʾahā wa-idhā bi-al-jāriyati aqbalat wa-hiya taltafitu yamīnan wa-shimālan
sentences.l: And when he-had-read-it, and behold, the slave-girl came-up, and she (was) turning right and left.
sentences.i: When he had read it, the slave-girl came up, looking this way and that.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-…, “and behold …”: after idhā of surprise, bi- only marks what appears. Classical Arabic would answer lammā without the wa-; the print's wa-idhā is a common construction in the Nights. iltafata (Form VIII), “to turn and look”; yamīnan wa-shimālan, “right and left”, are adverbial accusatives. The hamza of قرأها is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَرَأَتِ الْوَرَقَةَ فِي يَدِ الْجَوْهَرِيِّ فَقَالَتْ لَهُ يَا سَيِّدِي إِنَّ هَذِهِ الْوَرَقَةَ وَقَعَتْ مِنِّي
sentences.tr: fa-raʾati al-waraqata fī yadi al-jawhariyyi fa-qālat lahu yā sayyidī inna hādhihi al-waraqata waqaʿat minnī
sentences.l: And she-saw the paper in the hand of the jeweller, and she-said to-him: O my-master, this paper fell from-me.
sentences.i: She saw the letter in the jeweller's hand and said to him, “Sir, I dropped that letter.”
sentences.n: waqaʿa min, “to fall from”: waqaʿat minnī, “it fell from me”, is the Arabic way of saying “I dropped it”. inna simply opens the statement; the word after it is accusative. The hamza of فرأت is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمْ يَرُدَّ عَلَيْهَا جَوَابًا وَمَشَى وَمَشَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ خَلْفَهُ إِلَى أَنْ أَقْبَلَ عَلَى دَارِهِ وَدَخَلَ وَالْجَارِيَةُ خَلْفَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lam yarudda ʿalayhā jawāban wa-mashā wa-mashati al-jāriyatu khalfahu ilā an aqbala ʿalā dārihi wa-dakhala wa-al-jāriyatu khalfahu
sentences.l: And he-did-not return to-her an answer, and walked on; and the slave-girl walked behind-him, until he came-up to his-house and entered, and the slave-girl (was) behind-him.
sentences.i: He gave her no answer and walked on, and the slave-girl walked after him until he reached his house and went in, with her still behind him.
sentences.n: radda ʿalā … jawāban, “to give back an answer to”: the verb takes ʿalā for the person answered. ilā an, “until”, with a perfect here for what actually happened. aqbala ʿalā, “to come up to, arrive at”. wa-al-jāriyatu khalfahu, “the slave-girl behind him”, is a circumstantial clause without a verb.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ يَا سَيِّدِي أَعْطِنِي هَذِهِ الْوَرَقَةَ وَرُدَّ لِي فَإِنَّهَا سَقَطَتْ مِنِّي
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu yā sayyidī aʿṭinī hādhihi al-waraqata wa-rudda lī fa-innahā saqaṭat minnī
sentences.l: And she-said to-him: O my-master, give-me this paper and return (it) to-me, for it fell from-me.
sentences.i: She said to him, “Sir, give me that letter, give it back to me, for I dropped it.”
sentences.n: aʿṭinī, “give me”, imperative of Form IV aʿṭā. rudda lī, “return (it) to me”, imperative of radda; the object is understood, and li- marks the one it goes back to. The shadda of وردّ is the print's own. fa-innahā, “for it …”, gives the reason.

sentences.t: فَالْتَفَتَ إِلَيْهَا وَقَالَ يَا جَارِيَةَ الْخَيْرِ لَا تَخَافِي وَلَاتَحْزَنِي فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ سَتَّارٌ يُحِبُّ السَّتْرَ
sentences.tr: fa-iltafata ilayhā wa-qāla yā jāriyata al-khayri lā takhāfī wa-lā taḥzanī fa-inna Allāha sattārun yuḥibbu al-satra
sentences.l: And he-turned to-her and said: O girl of the good, do-not fear and do-not grieve, for God (is) a coverer, (who) loves the covering.
sentences.i: He turned to her and said, “My good girl, do not be afraid and do not be sad. God veils our faults and loves that they be veiled.
sentences.n: yā jāriyata al-khayri, “O girl of goodness”, a kindly form of address. lā with the jussive forbids: lā takhāfī, lā taḥzanī (the feminine ending -ī without its nūn); the print runs the second lā onto its verb (ولاتحزني), and the spacing is kept. sattār, “one who covers much”, the intensive pattern faʿʿāl from satara, “to cover, conceal”: God hides people's sins and secrets, and so should a man. The shaddas of ستّار and يحبّ are the print's own; yuḥibbu al-satra, “(who) loves covering”, describes God without a word for “who”.

sentences.t: فَأَخْبِرِينِي بِالْخَبَرِ عَلَى وَجْهِ الصِّدْقِ فَإِنِّي كَتُومٌ لِلْأَسْرَارِ وَلَكِنْ أُحَلِّفُكِ يَمِينًا أَنَّكِ لَاتُخْفِي عَنِّي شَيْأً مِنْ أَمْرِ سَيِّدَتِكِ
sentences.tr: fa-akhbirīnī bi-al-khabari ʿalā wajhi al-ṣidqi fa-innī katūmun li-al-asrāri wa-lākin uḥallifuki yamīnan annaki lā tukhfī ʿannī shayʾan min amri sayyidatiki
sentences.l: So tell-me the story in the way of the truth, for I (am) a keeper of the secrets; but I-make-you-swear an oath that you-will-not hide from-me a thing of the affair of your-mistress.
sentences.i: So tell me the whole story truthfully, for I keep secrets well. But I will have you swear that you will hide nothing from me of your mistress's affairs.
sentences.n: akhbara bi-, “to tell (someone) of”: the verb chooses bi- for what is told. ʿalā wajhi al-ṣidqi, “on the face of truth”, truthfully. katūm, “close, secret-keeping”, an intensive pattern from katama, “to hide”; li- marks what he keeps. ḥallafa (Form II), “to make someone swear”, with yamīnan, “an oath”, as a second object. annaki lā tukhfī: Classical Arabic wants tukhfīna here, since nothing calls for the jussive; dropping the nūn of the feminine indicative is Middle Arabic. The print runs lā onto its verb (لاتخفي) and spells shayʾ with its hamza on an alif (شيأ), both kept.

sentences.t: فَعَسَى اللَّهُ أَنْ يُعِينَنِي عَلَى قَضَاءِ أَغْرَاضِهَا وَيُسَهِّلَ الْأُمُورَ الصِّعَابَ عَلَى يَدِي
sentences.tr: fa-ʿasā Allāhu an yuʿīnanī ʿalā qaḍāʾi aghrāḍihā wa-yusahhila al-umūra al-ṣiʿāba ʿalā yadī
sentences.l: And perhaps God (will) help-me to the accomplishing of her-aims and make-easy the matters, the hard-ones, at my-hand.
sentences.i: It may be that God will help me bring about what she desires and smooth the hard way by my hand.”
sentences.n: ʿasā, “it may be”, takes an with the subjunctive: an yuʿīnanī, wa-yusahhila. aʿāna ʿalā (Form IV), “to help with”: the verb takes ʿalā for the task. qaḍāʾ, “carrying out, fulfilling”; aghrāḍ, plural of gharaḍ, “aim, wish”. ṣiʿāb, plural of ṣaʿb, “difficult”. ʿalā yadī, “at my hand”, through me.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ كَلَامَهُ قَالَتْ لَهُ يَا سَيِّدِي مَا ضَاعَ سِرٌّ أَنْتَ حَافِظُهُ وَلَاخَابَ أَمْرٌ أَنْتَ تَسْعَى فِي قَضَائِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿati al-jāriyatu kalāmahu qālat lahu yā sayyidī mā ḍāʿa sirrun anta ḥāfiẓuhu wa-lā khāba amrun anta tasʿā fī qaḍāʾihi
sentences.l: And when the slave-girl heard his-speech, she-said to-him: O my-master, no secret is lost (that) you (are) its-keeper, and no affair failed (that) you strive in its-accomplishing.
sentences.i: When the slave-girl heard what he said, she answered, “Sir, no secret is lost that you keep, and nothing fails that you work to bring about.
sentences.n: mā and lā with the perfect make timeless general statements, “never is a secret lost …”, almost a proverb. anta ḥāfiẓuhu, “you are its keeper”, and anta tasʿā fī qaḍāʾihi, “you strive for its fulfilment”, describe the indefinite nouns without a word for “that”; the -hu points back. khāba, “to fail, be disappointed”; saʿā fī, “to work at, strive for”. The print runs lā onto khāba (ولاخاب); the shadda of سرّ and the hamza of قضائه are its own.

sentences.t: اعْلَمْ أَنَّ قَلْبِي مَالَ إِلَيْكَ وَأَكْشِفُ خَبَرِى عَلَيْكَ وَأَعْطِنِى الْوَرَقَةَ
sentences.tr: iʿlam anna qalbī māla ilayka wa-akshifu khabarī ʿalayka wa-aʿṭinī al-waraqata
sentences.l: Know that my-heart has-inclined to-you, and I-uncover my-story to-you; and give-me the paper.
sentences.i: Know that my heart has warmed to you, and I will lay my story open before you. Now give me the letter.”
sentences.n: māla ilā, “to incline towards”, here to trust. The print's واكشف can be read as an imperative, “and uncover”, or as the first person akshifu, “and I uncover”; only the second fits a girl offering her story, so it is read so here. kashafa ʿalā, “to uncover to”, with ʿalā for the one shown. The print writes the -ī of خبرى and اعطنى with ى, a spelling habit of the edition.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَخْبَرَتْهُ بِجَمِيعِ الْخَبَرِ وَقَالَتِ اللَّهُ عَلَى مَا أَقُولُ شَهِيدٌ
sentences.tr: thumma akhbarathu bi-jamīʿi al-khabari wa-qālati Allāhu ʿalā mā aqūlu shahīdun
sentences.l: Then she-told-him of all the story and said: God (is) over what I-say a witness.
sentences.i: Then she told him the whole story and said, “God is witness to what I say.”
sentences.n: akhbara bi-, with bi- marking what is told. Allāhu ʿalā mā aqūlu shahīdun, “God is witness over what I say”, echoes a Qurʾānic oath formula (compare Qurʾān 12:66, Allāhu ʿalā mā naqūlu wakīl); shahīd ʿalā, “witness of”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا صَدَقْتِ فَإِنَّ عِنْدِى عِلْمًا بِأَصْلِ الْخَبَرِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā ṣadaqti fa-inna ʿindī ʿilman bi-aṣli al-khabari
sentences.l: And he-said to-her: You-have-spoken-truly, for with-me (is) knowledge of the root of the story.
sentences.i: He said to her, “You have told the truth, for I know how the story began.”
sentences.n: ṣadaqti, “you have spoken truly”, the perfect for a judgment on what was just said. fa-inna ʿindī ʿilman, “for with me is knowledge”: ʿilman is accusative after inna, its predicate ʿindī coming first. ʿilm bi-, “knowledge of”. aṣl, “root, origin”. The print writes عندى with ى.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ حَدَّثَهَا بِحَدِيثِ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَكَيْفَ أَخَذَ ضَمِيرَهُ وَأَخْبَرَهَا بِالْخَبَرِ مِنْ أَوَّلِهِ إِلَى آخِرِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma ḥaddathahā bi-ḥadīthi ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-kayfa akhadha ḍamīrahu wa-akhbarahā bi-al-khabari min awwalihi ilā ākhirihi
sentences.l: Then he-told-her the tale of ʿAlī son of Bakkār, and how he-took his-inmost-thought, and told-her the story from its-beginning to its-end.
sentences.i: Then he told her about ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, and how he had won his confidence, and told her everything from beginning to end.
sentences.n: ḥaddatha bi-, “to tell (someone) of”: the verb takes bi- for the tale; the shadda of حدّثها is the print's own. akhadha ḍamīrahu, “he took his inner mind”: ḍamīr is what one keeps hidden in one's heart, and the phrase seems to mean that the jeweller drew ʿAlī's secret out of him; it could also mean that ʿAlī had confided in him. The hamza of آخره is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ ذَلِكَ فَرِحَتْ وَاتَّفَقَا عَلَى أَنَّهَا تَأْخُذُ الْوَرَقَةَ وَتُعْطِيهَا لِعَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَبِجَمِيعِ مَايَجْرِي تَرْجِعُ إِلَيْهِ وَتُخْبِرُهُ بِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat dhālika fariḥat wa-ittafaqā ʿalā annahā taʾkhudhu al-waraqata wa-tuʿṭīhā li-ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-bi-jamīʿi mā yajrī tarjiʿu ilayhi wa-tukhbiruhu bihi
sentences.l: And when she-heard that, she-rejoiced; and they-two-agreed on that she takes the paper and gives-it to-ʿAlī son of Bakkār, and with all what happens she-returns to-him and tells-him of-it.
sentences.i: When she heard this she was glad, and the two agreed that she would take the letter and give it to ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, and come back to the jeweller with everything that happened and tell him of it.
sentences.n: ittafaqā, “the two agreed” (Form VIII, dual), with ʿalā for what is agreed. tuʿṭīhā li-…: li- marks the one she gives it to. wa-bi-jamīʿi mā yajrī … tukhbiruhu bihi: “all that happens” is put first for weight and picked up again by bihi, “of it”; akhbara bi-, the verb choosing bi- for what is told. ilayhi, “to him”, is the jeweller. jarā, “to run”, is also “to happen”; the print runs mā onto yajrī (مايجري), kept. The hamza of تأخذ is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَأَعْطَاهَا الْوَرَقَةَ فَأَخَذَتْهَا وَخَتَمَتْهَا كَمَا كَانَتْ
sentences.tr: fa-aʿṭāhā al-waraqata fa-akhadhathā wa-khatamathā kamā kānat
sentences.l: And he-gave-her the paper, and she-took-it and sealed-it as it had-been.
sentences.i: He gave her the letter, and she took it and sealed it up again as it had been.
sentences.n: aʿṭā (Form IV) takes two objects, the person and the thing. khatama, “to seal”: the letter had been closed with a seal, which the jeweller had broken to read it.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ إِنَّ سَيِّدَتِي شَمْسَ النَّهَارِ أَعْطَتْهَا لِي مَخْتُومَةً فَإِذَا قَرَأَهَا وَرَدَّ لِي جَوَابَهَا أَتَيْتُكَ بِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat inna sayyidatī Shamsa al-Nahāri aʿṭathā lī makhtūmatan fa-idhā qaraʾahā wa-radda lī jawābahā ataytuka bihi
sentences.l: And she-said: My-mistress Shams al-Nahār gave-it to-me sealed; so when he-reads-it and returns to-me its-answer, I-(shall)-come-to-you with-it.
sentences.i: And she said, “My mistress Shams al-Nahār gave it to me sealed. When he has read it and given me his answer, I will bring it to you.”
sentences.n: makhtūmatan, “sealed”, describes the letter's state (a ḥāl, in the accusative). aʿṭathā lī, “she gave it to me”, with li- for the receiver, a looser construction than aʿṭā's two objects. idhā with perfects looks to the future: “when he has read it … I shall bring it”. atā bi-, “to come with, bring”: bi- marks what is brought. The hamza of قرأها and the shadda of وردّ are the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ وَدَّعَتْهُ وَمَضَتْ إِلَي عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ فَوَجَدَتْهُ فِى الِانْتِظَارِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-jāriyata waddaʿathu wa-maḍat ilā ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin fa-wajadathu fī al-intiẓāri
sentences.l: Then the slave-girl bade-him-farewell and went to ʿAlī son of Bakkār, and she-found-him in the waiting.
sentences.i: Then the slave-girl took her leave of him and went to ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, whom she found waiting for her.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then indeed”, a storyteller's way of moving on; the noun after inna is accusative. fī al-intiẓār, “in (a state of) waiting”: intiẓār is the verbal noun of Form VIII intaẓara, “to wait”.

sentences.t: فَأَعْطَتْهُ الْوَرَقَةَ وَقَرَأَهَا ثُمَّ كَتَبَ لَهَا وَرَقَةَ رَدِّ الْجَوَابِ وَأَعْطَاهَا لَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-aʿṭathu al-waraqata wa-qaraʾahā thumma kataba lahā waraqata raddi al-jawābi wa-aʿṭāhā lahā
sentences.l: And she-gave-him the paper and he-read-it; then he-wrote for-her a paper of the returning of the answer, and gave-it to-her.
sentences.i: She gave him the letter, and he read it; then he wrote a reply for her and handed it to her.
sentences.n: waraqat radd al-jawāb, “a paper of the returning of the answer”, is simply a written reply. kataba lahā: li- may be “for her” to carry, or “to her”, Shams al-Nahār; the sense comes to the same. aʿṭāhā lahā, “he gave it to her”, again with li- for the receiver. The hamza of قرأها and the shadda of ردّ are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَتْهَا وَرَجَعَتْ بِهَا إِلَى الْجَوْهَرِيِّ فَأَخَذَ مِنْهَا وَفَضَّ خَتْمَهَا وَقَرَأَهَا فَوَجَدَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ فِيهَا مَكْتُوبًا هَذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhathā wa-rajaʿat bihā ilā al-jawhariyyi fa-akhadha minhā wa-faḍḍa khatmahā wa-qaraʾahā fa-wajada al-jawhariyyu fīhā maktūban hādhayni al-baytayni
sentences.l: And she-took-it and returned with-it to the jeweller; and he-took (it) from-her and broke its-seal and read-it, and the jeweller found in-it written these two verses:
sentences.i: She took it and went back with it to the jeweller. He took it from her, broke the seal and read it, and found these two lines of verse written there:
sentences.n: rajaʿa bi-, “to come back with”: bi- marks what she carries. faḍḍa al-khatm, “to break the seal”. wajada … maktūban hādhayni al-baytayni, “he found, written, these two verses”: here hādhayni al-baytayni is the object of wajada, in the accusative, and maktūban describes them. At the start of this passage the same thought was put with the verses in the nominative (raʾā maktūban fīhā hādhāni al-baytāni). The hamza of قرأها is the print's own.

sentences.t:
اِنَّ الرَّسُوْلَ الَّذِي كَانَتْ رَسَائِلُنَا * مَكْتُوْمَةٌ عِنْدَهُ ضَاعَتْ وَقَدْ غَضَبَا
فَاسْتَخْلِصُوْا الِيْ رَسُوْلاً مِنْكُمُ ثِقَةً * يَسْتَحْسِنُ الصِّدْقَ لَا يَسْتَحْسِنُ الْكَذِبَا
sentences.tr:
inna al-rasūla alladhī kānat rasāʾilunā * maktūmatun ʿindahu ḍāʿat wa-qad ghaḍabā
fa-istakhliṣū ilī rasūlan minkumu thiqatan * yastaḥsinu al-ṣidqa lā yastaḥsinu al-kadhibā
sentences.l:
Truly the messenger, with whom our letters were hidden-away, * (they) were-lost, and he has grown-angry;
so pick-out for-me a messenger from-you, trustworthy, * who approves the truth, does-not approve the lie.
sentences.i:
The messenger who kept our letters hidden has lost them, and now is angry;
so choose me from among you a trusty messenger, one who loves the truth and has no love for lies.
sentences.n: Metre: basīṭ. The pointing is the print's own, kept as printed, including the bare alif of اِنَّ and الِيْ, where the edition marks no hamza, and the sukūn it sets on long vowels (رَسُوْلَ, مَكْتُوْمَةٌ). Some printed vowels are not Classical: مَكْتُوْمَةٌ is nominative where the predicate of kānat would be accusative (maktūmatan), غَضَبَا is pointed ghaḍaba for Classical ghaḍiba, “he grew angry”, and الِيْ, read ilī, stands for ilayya, “to me, for me”. The final -ā of ghaḍabā and al-kadhibā is the lengthened vowel of the rhyme. The syntax is loose: inna al-rasūla, “the messenger”, is left hanging while ḍāʿat, “they were lost” (feminine, agreeing with rasāʾilunā, “our letters”), takes over; ʿAlī seems to mean the lost letter and the slave-girl, the messenger, angry at being accused (rasūl is masculine, hence ghaḍaba). istakhlaṣa (Form X), “to pick out, choose as one's own”. minkumu, with the old long plural ending -mu, fills out the metre. istaḥsana (Form X), “to find good, approve of”.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدُ فَإِنَّنِي مَا أَتَيْتُ بِخِيَانَةٍ * وَلَا ضَيَّعْتُ أَمَانَةً * وَلَمْ يَصْدُرْ مِنِّي جَفَاءٌ * وَلَا تَرَكْتُ وَفَاءً * وَلَا نَقَضْتُ عَهْدًا * وَلَا قَطَعْتُ وُدًّا * وَلَا فَارَقْتُ أَسَفًا *
sentences.tr: wa-baʿdu fa-innanī mā ataytu bi-khiyānatin * wa-lā ḍayyaʿtu amānatan * wa-lam yaṣdur minnī jafāʾun * wa-lā taraktu wafāʾan * wa-lā naqaḍtu ʿahdan * wa-lā qaṭaʿtu wuddan * wa-lā fāraqtu asafan *
sentences.l: And after: for I have-not come with a-betrayal, * nor lost a-trust, * and there has-not issued from-me harshness, * nor have-I left faithfulness, * nor broken a-pledge, * nor cut-off love, * nor parted-from grief. *
sentences.i: To proceed: I have committed no betrayal, * squandered no trust; * no harshness has come from me, * no faith have I forsaken, * no pledge have I broken, * no love have I severed, * nor has grief ever left me. *
sentences.n: The letter is in rhymed prose (sajʿ), and the print marks the end of each rhyming phrase with an asterisk. The rhymes come in pairs: khiyāna / amāna, jafāʾ / wafāʾ, ʿahdan / wuddan, and asafan opens the next pair with talafan. wa-baʿdu, “and after”, is the letter-writer's formula for passing from the greeting to the business. atā bi-, “to come with”, here “to commit”: the verb chooses bi-, which marks what is brought. ṣadara min, “to issue from”. fāraqtu asafan, “I have not parted from grief”: grief has not left him since the separation.

sentences.t: وَلَا لَقِيتُ بَعْدَ الْفِرَاقِ إِلَّا تَلَفًا * وَلَا عَلِمْتُ أَصْلًا بِمَا ذَكَرْتُمْ * وَلَا أُحِبُّ غَيْرَ مَا أَحْبَبْتُمْ *
sentences.tr: wa-lā laqītu baʿda al-firāqi illā talafan * wa-lā ʿalimtu aṣlan bi-mā dhakartum * wa-lā uḥibbu ghayra mā aḥbabtum *
sentences.l: And I-have-not met after the parting anything-except ruin, * nor knew-I at-all of-what you-mentioned, * nor do-I-love other-than what you-loved. *
sentences.i: Since the parting I have met with nothing but ruin; * of what you speak of I knew nothing at all; * and I love nothing but what you love. *
sentences.n: lā … illā, “not … except”, means “only”. aṣlan, “at all”, strengthens a negative. ʿalima bi-, “to know of, be aware of”: the verb chooses bi-. mā dhakartum, “what you mentioned”, is the suspicion that he sent Abū al-Ḥasan away to Basra. The plural “you” (-tum) is the polite plural for the one addressed. The rhyme is now -tum: dhakartum / aḥbabtum.

sentences.t: وَحَقِّ عَالِمِ السِّرِّ وَالنَّجْوَى * مَا قَصْدِي إِلَّا أَنْ أَجْتَمِعَ بِمَنْ أَهْوَى *
sentences.tr: wa-ḥaqqi ʿālimi al-sirri wa-al-najwā * mā qaṣdī illā an ajtamiʿa bi-man ahwā *
sentences.l: And (by) the right of the Knower of the secret and the whispered-talk, * my-aim is-not except that I-meet with-whom I-love. *
sentences.i: By the Knower of every secret and every whispered word, * my only aim is to be with the one I love. *
sentences.n: wa-ḥaqqi, “by the right of”, is an oath, wa- governing the genitive. ʿĀlim al-sirr wa-al-najwā, “Knower of the secret and the private talk”, is God. ijtamaʿa bi-, “to meet with, be united with”: the verb chooses bi-. hawā, “to love, be passionately fond of”. Rhyme: najwā / ahwā.

sentences.t: وَشَأْنِي كِتْمَانُ الْغَرَامِ * وَإِنْ أَمْرَضَنِى السَّقَامُ * وَهَذَا شَرْحُ حَالِي وَالسَّلَامُ *
sentences.tr: wa-shaʾnī kitmānu al-gharāmi * wa-in amraḍanī al-saqāmu * wa-hādhā sharḥu ḥālī wa-al-salāmu *
sentences.l: And my-way (is) the concealing of the passion, * even-if the sickness has-made-me-ill; * and this (is) the explaining of my-state, and peace. *
sentences.i: My way is to keep my passion hidden, * though sickness has laid me low. * This is the account of how things stand with me; and peace be with you. *
sentences.n: wa-in, “and if”, here “even if”. amraḍa (Form IV), “to make ill”; the print writes the suffix -nī with ى (أمرضنى), one of its spelling habits. The last rhyme is gharām / saqām / salām, and wa-al-salām, “and peace”, is the usual close of a letter.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا قَرَأَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ هَذِهِ الرُّقْعَةَ وَعَرَفَ مَا فِيهَا بَكَى بُكَاءً شَدِيدًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā qaraʾa al-jawhariyyu hādhihi al-ruqʿata wa-ʿarafa mā fīhā bakā bukāʾan shadīdan
sentences.l: And when the jeweller read this note and knew what (was) in-it, he-wept a-weeping severe.
sentences.i: When the jeweller had read this note and understood what was in it, he wept bitterly.
sentences.n: bakā bukāʾan shadīdan, “he wept a hard weeping”: the verb with its own verbal noun (an absolute object), qualified by an adjective, is the usual way of saying “very much”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ قَالَتْ لَهُ لَا تَخْرُجْ عَنْ هَذَا الْمَكَانِ حَتَّى أَعُودَ إِلَيْكَ لِأَنَّهُ قَدِ اتَّهَمَنِي بِأَمْرٍ مِنَ الْأُمُورِ وَهُوَ مَعْذُورٌ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-jāriyata qālat lahu lā takhruj ʿan hādhā al-makāni ḥattā aʿūda ilayka li-annahu qadi ittahamanī bi-amrin mina al-umūri wa-huwa maʿdhūrun
sentences.l: Then the slave-girl said to-him: Do-not go-out from this place until I-return to-you, because he has accused-me of-a-matter of the matters, and he (is) excused.
sentences.i: Then the slave-girl said to him, “Do not leave this place until I come back to you. He has accused me of something, and he cannot be blamed for it.
sentences.n: lā takhruj, “do not go out”: lā with the jussive is a prohibition. ḥattā aʿūda, “until I return”, takes the subjunctive. ittahama (Form VIII) … bi-, “to accuse someone of”: the verb chooses bi-, which marks the charge. “He” is ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, who has accused her of losing his letter; maʿdhūr, “excused”, means he has good reason.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَجْمَعَ بَيْنَكَ وَبَيْنَ سَيِّدَتِي شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ بِأَيِّ حِيلَةٍ كَانَتْ فَإِنِّي تَرَكْتُهَا مَطْرُوحَةً وَهِيَ تَنْتَظِرُ مِنِّي رَدَّ الْجَوَابِ
sentences.tr: wa-anā urīdu an ajmaʿa baynaka wa-bayna sayyidatī Shamsi al-Nahāri bi-ayyi ḥīlatin kānat fa-innī taraktuhā maṭrūḥatan wa-hiya tantaẓiru minnī radda al-jawābi
sentences.l: And I want that I-bring-together between-you and between my-mistress Shams al-Nahār by any stratagem it-was; for I left-her cast-down, and she awaits from-me the return of the answer.
sentences.i: I mean to bring you and my mistress Shams al-Nahār together by whatever means it takes; for I left her lying prostrate, waiting for me to bring back the answer.”
sentences.n: jamaʿa bayna … wa-bayna, “to bring together”, repeating bayna with each party. bi-ayyi ḥīlatin kānat, “by whatever stratagem it may be”: bi- is “by, by means of”, and ayy with kānat makes the generalising “any … at all”. maṭrūḥa, “cast down”, is said of someone lying ill with love. radd al-jawāb, “the returning of the answer”, is the reply to a letter.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ مَضَتْ إِلَى سَيِّدَتِهَا وَبَاتَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ مُشَوَّشَ الْخَاطِرِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-jāriyata maḍat ilā sayyidatihā wa-bāta al-jawhariyyu mushawwasha al-khāṭiri
sentences.l: Then the slave-girl went to her-mistress, and the jeweller spent-the-night disturbed of the mind.
sentences.i: Then the slave-girl went off to her mistress, and the jeweller passed the night with his mind in turmoil.
sentences.n: bāta, “to spend the night”, is one of the sisters of kāna, so its predicate mushawwasha is accusative. mushawwash al-khāṭir, “troubled of mind”, is an adjective with a following genitive naming the part affected.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ صَلَّى الصُّبْحَ وَقَعَدَ يَنْتَظِرُ قُدُومَهَا وَإِذَا بِهَا أَقْبَلَتْ وَهِيَ فَرْحَانَةٌ إِلَى أَنْ دَخَلَتْ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu ṣallā al-ṣubḥa wa-qaʿada yantaẓiru qudūmahā wa-idhā bihā aqbalat wa-hiya farḥānatun ilā an dakhalat ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And when the morning dawned, he-prayed the dawn (prayer) and sat-down awaiting her-arrival; and behold her, she-came-up, and she (was) glad, until she entered upon-him.
sentences.i: When morning came he said the dawn prayer and sat waiting for her to come; and presently there she was, coming towards him full of joy, until she came in to him.
sentences.n: aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥ, “the morning dawned”, a formula of the tales. al-ṣubḥ is the dawn prayer. wa-idhā bihā, “and behold, she”: after idhā of surprise, bi- only marks the one who appears. farḥāna, “glad”, is a colloquial-leaning feminine of farḥān; Classical prefers farḥā. dakhala ʿalā, “to go in to” someone, the verb choosing ʿalā.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا مَا الْخَبَرُ يَا جَارِيَةُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā mā al-khabaru yā jāriyatu
sentences.l: And he-said to-her: What (is) the news, O slave-girl?
sentences.i: He said to her, “What news, girl?”

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ مَضَيْتُ مِنْ عِنْدِكَ إِلَى سَيِّدَتِي وَدَفَعْتُ لَهَا الرُّقْعَةَ الَّتِي كَتَبَهَا عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ فَلَمَّا قَرَأَتْهَا وَفَهِمَتْ مَعْنَاهَا حَارَتْ فِي فِكْرِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat maḍaytu min ʿindika ilā sayyidatī wa-dafaʿtu lahā al-ruqʿata allatī katabahā ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin fa-lammā qaraʾathā wa-fahimat maʿnāhā ḥārat fī fikrihā
sentences.l: And she-said: I-went from at-you to my-mistress and handed to-her the note which ʿAlī son of Bakkār wrote; and when she-read-it and understood its-meaning, she-was-bewildered in her-thought.
sentences.i: She said, “I went from you to my mistress and gave her the note ʿAlī ibn Bakkār had written. When she had read it and understood what it meant, she was at a loss what to think.
sentences.n: min ʿindika, “from beside you”: ʿind, “at, with”, after min gives “from (someone's place)”. dafaʿa li-, “to hand to”, with li- marking the receiver; Classical more often uses ilā. ḥārat fī fikrihā, “she was perplexed in her thought”: ḥāra (hollow verb), “to be bewildered”.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهَا يَا سَيِّدَتِي لَا تَخْشَيْ مِنْ فَسَادِ الْأَمْرِ بَيْنَكُمَا بِسَبَبِ غِيَابِ أَبِي الْحَسَنِ فَإِنِّي وَجَدْتُ مَنْ يَقُومُ مَقَامَهُ وَهُوَ أَحْسَنُ مِنْهُ وَأَعْلَى مِقْدَارًا وَأَهْلًا لِكِتْمَانِ الْأَسْرَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahā yā sayyidatī lā takhshay min fasādi al-amri baynakumā bi-sababi ghiyābi Abī al-Ḥasani fa-innī wajadtu man yaqūmu maqāmahu wa-huwa aḥsanu minhu wa-aʿlā miqdāran wa-ahlan li-kitmāni al-asrāri
sentences.l: And I-said to-her: O my-mistress, do-not fear of the spoiling of the matter between-you-two because of the absence of Abū al-Ḥasan, for I have-found one-who stands (in) his-place, and he (is) better than-him and higher (in) rank, and fitting for-the-keeping of the secrets.
sentences.i: So I said to her, ‘My lady, do not fear that things between the two of you will go wrong because Abū al-Ḥasan is gone. I have found someone to take his place, a better man than he, of higher standing, and well fit to keep secrets.’
sentences.n: lā takhshay, “do not fear”, is the feminine jussive (takhshay-na with its ending dropped); khashiya min, “to be afraid of”. baynakumā, “between you two”, is dual. qāma maqāmahu, “to stand in his stead”. aʿlā miqdāran, “higher in rank”: the accusative after the comparative says in what respect. wa-ahlan, “and worthy”, is accusative although it continues the predicate aḥsanu, which is nominative; it seems drawn into the accusative of miqdāran just before. ahl li-, “worthy of, fit for”: li- names what he is fit for.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ حَدَّثْتُهَا بِمَا بَيْنَكَ وَبَيْنَ أَبِي الْحَسَنِ وَكَيْفَ تَوَصَّلْتُ إِلَيْهِ وَإِلَى عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَكَيْفَ سَقَطَتْ تِلْكَ الرُّقْعَةُ مِنِّي وَقَدْ وَقَعْتَ أَنْتَ عَلَيْهَا وَأَخْبَرْتُهَا بِمَا اسْتَقَرَّ عَلَيْهِ الْأَمْرُ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-qad ḥaddathtuhā bi-mā baynaka wa-bayna Abī al-Ḥasani wa-kayfa tawaṣṣaltu ilayhi wa-ilā ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-kayfa saqaṭat tilka al-ruqʿatu minnī wa-qad waqaʿta anta ʿalayhā wa-akhbartuhā bi-mā istaqarra ʿalayhi al-amru baynī wa-baynaka
sentences.l: And I-have told-her of-what (is) between-you and between Abū al-Ḥasan, and how I-made-my-way to-him and to ʿAlī son of Bakkār, and how that note fell from-me and you, you-came upon-it; and I-informed-her of-what the matter settled upon between-me and between-you.
sentences.i: I told her how things stood between you and Abū al-Ḥasan, how I had found my way to him and to ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, and how that note fell from my hands and you came upon it; and I told her what you and I had agreed on.”
sentences.n: ḥaddatha (Form II) … bi-, “to tell someone of”, and akhbara (Form IV) … bi-, “to inform someone of”: both verbs choose bi-, which marks the thing told. tawaṣṣala ilā, “to find one's way to, gain access to”. waqaʿa ʿalā, “to fall upon, come across”; the print itself marks the fatḥa of waqaʿta, “you came upon”, and the added anta, “you”, stresses it. istaqarra ʿalā, “to settle on”: what the matter came to rest on, here what they agreed.

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ غَايَةَ الْعَجَبِ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjaba al-jawhariyyu ghāyata al-ʿajabi
sentences.l: And the jeweller marvelled the utmost of the marvelling.
sentences.i: The jeweller was utterly astonished.
sentences.n: ghāyata al-ʿajab, “the utmost of wonder”, stands in the accusative as an absolute object: “he wondered with the utmost wonder”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لَهُ إِنَّ سَيِّدَتِي تَشْتَهِي أَنْ تَسْمَعَ كَلَامَكَ لِأَجْلِ أَنْ تُؤَكِّدَ عَلَيْهِ فِيمَا بَيْنَكَ وَبَيْنَهُ مِنَ الْعُهُودِ فَاعْزِمْ عَلَى الْمَسِيرِ مَعِي إِلَيْهَا فِي هَذَا الْوَقْتِ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat lahu inna sayyidatī tashtahī an tasmaʿa kalāmaka li-ajli an tuʾakkida ʿalayhi fī-mā baynaka wa-baynahu mina al-ʿuhūdi fa-iʿzim ʿalā al-masīri maʿī ilayhā fī hādhā al-waqti
sentences.l: Then she-said to-him: My-mistress desires that she-hear your-speech, for-the-sake-of that she-make-firm upon-him in-what (is) between-you and between-him of the pledges; so resolve upon the going with-me to-her at this time.
sentences.i: Then she said to him, “My mistress longs to hear what you have to say, so that she may make sure of the pledges between you and him. So make up your mind to come with me to her now.”
sentences.n: li-ajli an, “for the sake of, in order that”: li- with ajl, “sake”. akkada ʿalā (Form II), “to press, insist upon, make binding on”. The pronoun of ʿalayhi, “on him”, is not quite clear: the likeliest reading is that “him” is ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, and that she wants to make sure through the jeweller of the agreements between him and ʿAlī. ʿazama ʿalā, “to resolve upon”, the verb choosing ʿalā. al-masīr, “going, setting off”, is a verbal noun of sāra.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ كَلَامَ الْجَارِيَةِ رَأٰةُ أَمْرًا عَظِيمًا وَخَطَرًا جَسِيمًا لَايُمْكِنُ الدُّخُولُ فِيهِ وَلَا التَّهَجُّمُ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-jawhariyyu kalāma al-jāriyati raʾāhu amran ʿaẓīman wa-khaṭaran jasīman lā yumkinu al-dukhūlu fīhi wa-lā al-tahajjumu ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And when the jeweller heard the slave-girl's speech, he-saw-it (as) a-matter enormous and a-danger grave, (which) it-is-not-possible the entering into-it nor the rushing upon-it.
sentences.i: When the jeweller heard what the slave-girl had to say, he saw it as a weighty business and a grave danger, something no one could enter into or rush headlong upon.
sentences.n: The print writes رأة for raʾāhu, “he saw it”, with ة standing for the pronoun ه, one of its spelling habits; here the long ā is not written either. raʾā with two accusatives, “to see something as”. ʿaẓīman / jasīman make a little rhyme. lā yumkinu, “it is not possible”, run together as one word in the print, takes al-dukhūl, “entering”, as its subject. tahajjama ʿalā (Form V), “to rush in upon, venture rashly into”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ لِلْجَارِيَةِ يَا أُخْتِي إِنِّي مِنْ أَوْلَادِ الْعَوَامِّ وَلَمْ أَكُنْ كَأَبِى الْحَسَنِ لِأَنَّ أَبَا الْحَسَنِ كَانَ رَفِيعَ الْمِقْدَارِ مَعْرُوفًا بِالِاشْتِهَارِ مُتَرَّدِّدًا عَلَى دَارِ الْخِلَافَةِ لِاحْتِيَاجِهِمْ إِلَى بِضَاعَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-jawhariyyu li-al-jāriyati yā ukhtī innī min awlādi al-ʿawāmmi wa-lam akun ka-Abī al-Ḥasani li-anna Abā al-Ḥasani kāna rafīʿa al-miqdāri maʿrūfan bi-al-ishtihāri mutaraddidan ʿalā dāri al-khilāfati li-iḥtiyājihim ilā biḍāʿatihi
sentences.l: And the jeweller said to-the slave-girl: O my-sister, I (am) of the sons of the common-people, and I-was-not like Abū al-Ḥasan, because Abū al-Ḥasan was high of rank, known for (his) renown, going-back-and-forth to the House of the Caliphate, because-of their-needing (of) his-wares.
sentences.i: The jeweller said to the slave-girl, “Sister, I am one of the common people; I am not like Abū al-Ḥasan. Abū al-Ḥasan was a man of high standing, widely known, and a regular visitor at the Caliph's palace, because they needed his wares.
sentences.n: awlād al-ʿawāmm, “sons of the commoners”, means “a man of the common people”. lam akun, literally “I was not”, here “I am not”. ka-Abī, “like Abū”: ka- is “like”, and Abū becomes Abī in the genitive (printed with ى here). The print sets the shadda of مترّددا on the rāʾ; the word is mutaraddid (Form V), “going to and fro, frequenting”, with taraddada ʿalā, “to visit regularly”, and the doubling belongs on the dāl. li-iḥtiyājihim ilā, “because of their need for”: li- gives the reason, and iḥtiyāj (Form VIII verbal noun) takes ilā. “They” are the people of the palace.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا أَنَا فَإِنَّ أَبَا الْحَسَنِ كَانَ يُحَدِّثُنِي وَأَنَا أَرْتَعِدُ مِنْ حَدِيثِهِ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā anā fa-inna Abā al-Ḥasani kāna yuḥaddithunī wa-anā artaʿidu min ḥadīthihi bayna yadayhi
sentences.l: And as-for me, Abū al-Ḥasan used-to talk-to-me, and I tremble from his-talk before his-hands.
sentences.i: As for me, when Abū al-Ḥasan used to tell me of it, I would tremble in his presence at what he said.
sentences.n: ammā … fa-, “as for … then”: the fa- opens the comment on the topic. kāna yuḥaddithunī, “he used to talk to me”: kāna with the imperfect for a habit in the past. wa-anā artaʿidu, “while I tremble”, a circumstantial clause. bayna yadayhi, “between his hands”, means “in front of him”.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا كَانَتْ سَيِّدَتُكِ رَغِبَتْ فِي حَدِيثِي لَهَا فَيَنْبَغِي أَنْ يَكُونَ ذَلِكَ فِى غَيْرِ دَارِ الْخِلَافَةِ بَعِيدًا عَنْ مَحَلِّ أَمِيرِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ لِأَنَّ عَقْلِي لَيْسَ يُطَاوِعُنِي عَلَى مَاتَقُولِينَ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā kānat sayyidatuki raghibat fī ḥadīthī lahā fa-yanbaghī an yakūna dhālika fī ghayri dāri al-khilāfati baʿīdan ʿan maḥalli amīri al-muʾminīna li-anna ʿaqlī laysa yuṭāwiʿunī ʿalā mā taqūlīna
sentences.l: And if your-mistress has-desired (it) in my-talking to-her, then it-is-fitting that that be in other-than the House of the Caliphate, far from the place of the Commander of the Faithful, because my-mind does-not comply-with-me on what-you-say.
sentences.i: If your mistress wishes me to speak with her, it ought to be somewhere other than the Caliph's palace, well away from where the Commander of the Faithful is; for my mind will not go along with what you propose.”
sentences.n: idhā kānat … raghibat, “if she has wished”: kāna with a perfect, a pluperfect-like “has come to wish”. raghiba fī, “to desire”, the verb choosing fī. yanbaghī an, “it is proper that, it ought to be that”. laysa yuṭāwiʿunī, “does not obey me”: laysa with an imperfect is a plain negative, common in this prose. ṭāwaʿa (Form III) … ʿalā, “to go along with someone in something”. mā taqūlīna, “what you (f.) say”, is run together in the print.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ امْتَنَعَ مِنَ الْمَسِيرِ مَعَهَا
sentences.tr: thumma innahu imtanaʿa mina al-masīri maʿahā
sentences.l: Then he refused from the going with-her.
sentences.i: And he refused to go with her.
sentences.n: imtanaʿa min (Form VIII), “to hold back from, refuse”: the verb chooses min. thumma innahu, “then he”, the story's usual way of moving on.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا الْجَارِيَةُ فَإِنَّهَا صَارَتْ تَتَضَمَّنُ لَهُ السَّلَامَةَ وَتَقُولُ لَهُ لَاتَخَفْ وَلَاتَخْشَ مِنْ ضَرَرٍ وَكَرَّرَتْ عَلَيْهِ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā al-jāriyatu fa-innahā ṣārat tataḍammanu lahu al-salāmata wa-taqūlu lahu lā takhaf wa-lā takhsha min ḍararin wa-karrarat ʿalayhi dhālika
sentences.l: And as-for the slave-girl, she began guaranteeing to-him the safety and saying to-him: Do-not-fear and do-not-dread of harm; and she-repeated to-him that.
sentences.i: But the slave-girl kept assuring him that he would be safe, saying, “Do not be afraid, have no fear of any harm,” and she said it to him over and over.
sentences.n: ṣārat tataḍammanu, “she began to guarantee”: ṣāra with the imperfect, “to set about, keep on doing”. taḍammana li- (Form V), “to guarantee to someone”, li- marking the one assured. lā takhaf and lā takhsha, run together in the print, are jussives of prohibition, with their long vowels shortened (khāfa > takhaf, khashiya > takhsha). karrara ʿalā (Form II), “to repeat to someone”.

sentences.t: فَهَمَّ أَنْ يَقُومَ مَعَهَا فَانْثَنَتْ رِجْلَاهُ وَارْتَعَشَتْ يَدَاهُ
sentences.tr: fa-hamma an yaqūma maʿahā fa-inthanat rijlāhu wa-irtaʿashat yadāhu
sentences.l: And he-was-about-to that he-rise with-her, and his-two-legs bent and his-two-hands shook.
sentences.i: He made to get up and go with her, but his legs gave way beneath him and his hands began to shake.
sentences.n: hamma an, “to be about to, set out to”. inthanā (Form VII), “to bend, fold”; irtaʿasha (Form VIII), “to tremble”. rijlāhu and yadāhu are duals, “his two legs”, “his two hands”, with the -ā of the nominative dual.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ حَاشَ اللَّهِ أَنْ أَذْهَبَ مَعَكِ وَلَيْسَ لِي قُدْرَةٌ عَلَى ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ḥāsha Allāhi an adhhaba maʿaki wa-laysa lī qudratun ʿalā dhālika
sentences.l: And he-said: Far-be (it) of God that I-go with-you, and there-is-not to-me power over that.
sentences.i: He said, “God forbid that I should go with you! I have not the strength for it.”
sentences.n: ḥāsha Allāhi, “God forbid”, an exclamation of refusal (also ḥāsha li-llāhi). laysa lī qudratun ʿalā, “I have no power for”: li- marks the possessor, and qudra takes ʿalā.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ الْجَارِيَهُ اطْمَئِنَّ قَلْبَكَ إِنْ كَانَ يَصْعُبُ عَلَيْكَ الرَّوَاحُ إِلَى دَارِ الْخِلَافَةِ وَلَايُمْكِنُكَ الْمَسِيرُ مَعِي فَأَنَا أَجْعَلُهَا تَسِيرُ إِلَيْكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu al-jāriyahu iṭmaʾinna qalbaka in kāna yaṣʿubu ʿalayka al-rawāḥu ilā dāri al-khilāfati wa-lā yumkinuka al-masīru maʿī fa-anā ajʿaluhā tasīru ilayka
sentences.l: And the slave-girl said to-him: Be-at-rest (as to) your-heart; if it-is hard upon-you the going to the House of the Caliphate and it-is-not-possible-for-you the going with-me, then I, I-will-make-her come to-you.
sentences.i: The slave-girl said to him, “Set your heart at rest. If it is too hard for you to go to the Caliph's palace, and you cannot come with me, then I will have her come to you.
sentences.n: The print has المشير, a misprint for المسير, corrected here. It writes al-jāriyah with ه for ة, one of its spelling habits. iṭmaʾinna qalbaka, “be at rest as to your heart”: an imperative of iṭmaʾanna, “to be tranquil”, with qalbaka as an accusative of respect; a Classical writer would say li-yaṭmaʾinna qalbuka, “let your heart be at rest”. kāna yaṣʿubu, “it is hard”, with al-rawāḥ, “going”, as subject; ṣaʿuba ʿalā, “to be hard for someone”. lā yumkinuka, “it is not possible for you”, run together in the print. jaʿala with an imperfect, “to make someone do”.

sentences.t: فَلَاتَبْرَحْ مِنْ مَكَانِكَ حَتَّى أَرْجِعَ إِلَيْكَ بِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lā tabraḥ min makānika ḥattā arjiʿa ilayka bihā
sentences.l: So do-not-leave from your-place until I-return to-you with-her.
sentences.i: So do not stir from where you are until I come back to you with her.”
sentences.n: lā tabraḥ, run together in the print, is a jussive of prohibition; bariḥa min, “to leave, quit (a place)”, here with min. rajaʿa bi-, “to come back with, bring back”: the verb chooses bi-, which marks what is brought.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ مَضَتْ وَلَمْ تَغِبْ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-jāriyata maḍat wa-lam taghib illā qalīlan
sentences.l: Then the slave-girl went, and she-was-not-absent except a-little.
sentences.i: Then the slave-girl went off, and was gone only a little while.
sentences.n: lam taghib, jussive of ghāba, “to be absent”, with its long vowel shortened. lam … illā qalīlan, “was not absent except a little”, means “was away only briefly”.

sentences.t: وَعَادَتْ إِلَى الْجَوْهَرِيِّ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ احْذَرْ مِنْ أَنْ يَكُونَ عِنْدَكَ أَحَدٌ غَيْرُكَ مِنْ غُلَامٍ أَوْ جَارِيَةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿādat ilā al-jawhariyyi wa-qālat lahu iḥdhar min an yakūna ʿindaka aḥadun ghayruka min ghulāmin aw jāriyatin
sentences.l: And she-returned to the jeweller and said to-him: Beware of that there-be with-you anyone other-than-you, of boy or slave-girl.
sentences.i: Then she went back to the jeweller and said to him, “Take care that there is no one in the house with you besides yourself, neither page nor slave-girl.”
sentences.n: ḥadhira min, “to beware of”, the verb choosing min; what is to be avoided follows as an an-clause with the subjunctive (an yakūna). ʿindaka, “with you”, here “in your house”. min ghulāmin aw jāriyatin: min spells out what kind of “anyone” is meant.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا مَاعِنْدِي غَيْرُ جَارِيَةٍ سَوْدَاءَ كَبِيرَةِ السِّنِّ تَخْلُ مِنِّي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā mā ʿindī ghayru jāriyatin sawdāʾa kabīrati al-sinni takhlu minnī
sentences.l: And he-said to-her: Not-with-me (is anyone) except a slave-girl, black, great of age, (who) serves me.
sentences.i: He said to her, “I have no one but an old black slave-woman who serves me.”
sentences.n: The print has تخل مني, which makes no sense as it stands; it is probably a misprint for تخدمني, takhdumunī, “who serves me”, and the translation follows that guess. The print's two words are kept and pointed as they might be read. māʿindī, “there is not with me”, is set as one word in the print. kabīrat al-sinn, “great of age”, i.e. old: an adjective followed by a defining genitive. sawdāʾ, “black”, is diptote, hence the single fatḥa.

sentences.t: فَقَامَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ وَأَغْلَقَتِ الْبَابَ بَيْنَ جَارِيَةِ الْجَوْهَرِيِّ وَبَيْنَهُ وَصَرَفَتْ غِلْمَانَهُ إِلَى خَارِجِ الدَّارِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāmati al-jāriyatu wa-aghlaqati al-bāba bayna jāriyati al-jawhariyyi wa-baynahu wa-ṣarafat ghilmānahu ilā khāriji al-dāri
sentences.l: And the slave-girl rose and locked the door between the slave-girl of the jeweller and between-him, and sent-away his-pages to the outside of the house.
sentences.i: So the slave-girl got up and locked the door between the jeweller's slave-woman and him, and sent his pages out of the house.
sentences.n: bayna X wa-bayna-hu, “between X and him”: Arabic repeats bayna before a pronoun. ṣarafa, “to send away, dismiss”. ghilmān is the plural of ghulām, “page, serving boy”; the jeweller has just said he keeps only the old woman, but the story now gives him pages too.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ خَرَجَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ وَعَادَتْ وَمَعَهَا جَارِيَةٌ خَلْفَهَا وَدَخَلَتْ بِهَا دَارَ الْجَوْهَرِيِّ فَأَعْبَقَتِ الدَّارَ مِنَ الطِّيبِ
sentences.tr: thumma kharajati al-jāriyatu wa-ʿādat wa-maʿahā jāriyatun khalfahā wa-dakhalat bihā dāra al-jawhariyyi fa-aʿbaqati al-dāra mina al-ṭībi
sentences.l: Then the slave-girl went-out and returned, and with-her a slave-girl behind-her, and she-entered with-her the house of the jeweller; and she-filled-with-fragrance the house from the perfume.
sentences.i: Then the slave-girl went out and came back with another young woman following behind her, and brought her into the jeweller's house; and the house was filled with the scent of her perfume.
sentences.n: wa-maʿahā jāriyatun, “with another young woman with her”: a circumstantial clause without a verb. The second jāriya is Shams al-Nahār herself, a slave-girl of the Caliph, not yet named. dakhala bi-, “to bring in”: bi- with a verb of motion makes it “take along”. aʿbaqa (Form IV of ʿabiqa, “to cling, of a scent”), “to fill with fragrance”; min al-ṭīb, “with perfume”, names what the fragrance came from.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَآهَا الْجَوْهَرِيُّ نَهَضَ قَائِمًا وَوَضَعَ لَهَا مَرْتَبَةً وَمِخَدَّةً فَجَلَسَتْ عَلَيْهَا وَجَلَسَ هُوَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhā al-jawhariyyu nahaḍa qāʾiman wa-waḍaʿa lahā martabatan wa-mikhaddatan fa-jalasat ʿalayhā wa-jalasa huwa bayna yadayhā
sentences.l: And when the jeweller saw-her, he-rose standing, and placed for-her a mattress and a cushion; and she-sat on-it, and he sat, he, between her-two-hands.
sentences.i: When the jeweller saw her he sprang to his feet and set out a mattress and a cushion for her. She sat down on it, and he sat before her.
sentences.n: nahaḍa qāʾiman, “he rose standing”: the accusative participle underlines the verb, a common pairing. martaba is a floor mattress or seat, mikhadda a cushion for leaning on. bayna yadayhā, “between her two hands”, i.e. in front of her, the place of one who waits on another.

sentences.t: فَمَكَثَتْ سَاعَةً لَمْ تَتَكَلَّمْ حَتَّى أَخَذَتِ الرَّاحَةَ ثُمَّ كَشَفَتْ وَجْهَهَا فَخُيِّلَ لِلْجَوْهَرِيِّ أَنَّ الشَّمْسَ أَشْرَقَتْ فِي مَنْزِلِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-makathat sāʿatan lam tatakallam ḥattā akhadhati al-rāḥata thumma kashafat wajhahā fa-khuyyila li-al-jawhariyyi anna al-shamsa ashraqat fī manzilihi
sentences.l: And she-stayed an hour, she-did-not-speak, until she-took the rest; then she-uncovered her-face, and it-was-made-to-seem to-the-jeweller that the sun had-risen in his-dwelling.
sentences.i: For a while she sat without speaking, until she had rested; then she unveiled her face, and it seemed to the jeweller that the sun had risen in his house.
sentences.n: sāʿa, “hour”, often means just “a while”. akhadha al-rāḥa, “to take rest”, i.e. to recover one's breath. khuyyila li-, “it was made to seem to, it appeared to” (passive of Form II khayyala); li- marks the one who imagines it. The sun is a pointed comparison: her name, Shams al-Nahār, means “Sun of the Day”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لِجَارِيَتِهَا أَهَذَا الرَّجُلُ الَّذِي قُلْتِ لِي عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat li-jāriyatihā a-hādhā al-rajulu alladhī qulti lī ʿalayhi
sentences.l: Then she-said to-her-slave-girl: Is-this the man whom you-told me about-him?
sentences.i: Then she said to her slave-girl, “Is this the man you told me about?”
sentences.n: a-, the question prefix, on hādhā. qāla ʿalā, “to speak about, tell of”: Middle Arabic uses ʿalā where Classical would say ʿan. The -hi of ʿalayhi is the resumptive pronoun that a relative clause needs in Arabic (“whom you told me about him”).

sentences.t: قَالَتْ نَعَمْ فَالْتَفَتَتْ إِلَى الْجَوْهَرِيِّ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ كَيْفَ حَالُكَ قَالَ بِخَيْرٍ وَدُعَاءٍ فِي حَيَاتِكِ وَحَيَاةِ أَمِيرِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ
sentences.tr: qālat naʿam fa-iltafatat ilā al-jawhariyyi wa-qālat lahu kayfa ḥāluka qāla bi-khayrin wa-duʿāʾin fī ḥayātiki wa-ḥayāti amīri al-muʾminīna
sentences.l: She-said: Yes. And she-turned to the jeweller and said to-him: How (is) your-state? He-said: In good, and (in) prayer for your-life and the life of the Commander of the Faithful.
sentences.i: “Yes,” she said. Then she turned to the jeweller and said to him, “How are you?” He said, “Well, and praying for your life and the life of the Commander of the Faithful.”
sentences.n: bi-khayrin, “in good (health)”, the usual answer to kayfa ḥāluka; bi- here means “in (a state of)”. duʿāʾ fī ḥayātik, “prayer for your life”: Classical would more often say duʿāʾ li-, but fī, “concerning”, is also found. The Commander of the Faithful is the Caliph, Hārūn al-Rashīd, whose favourite Shams al-Nahār is.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ إِنَّكَ حَمَلْتَنَا عَلَى الْمَسِيرِ عِنْدَكَ وَأَنْ نُطْلِعَكَ عَلَى مَا يَكُونُ مِنْ سِرِّنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat innaka ḥamaltanā ʿalā al-masīri ʿindaka wa-an nuṭliʿaka ʿalā mā yakūnu min sirrinā
sentences.l: And she-said: Indeed you have-led-us to the going (to be) with-you, and that we-let-you-know of what may-be of our-secret.
sentences.i: She said, “It is you who have brought us to come to you here, and to let you into whatever secret of ours there may be.”
sentences.n: ḥamala ʿalā, “to bring someone to (doing) something, induce”, the verb choosing ʿalā. Its object is first a verbal noun, al-masīr, “going”, then an an-clause, an nuṭliʿaka, both governed by the one ʿalā. aṭlaʿa ʿalā (Form IV), “to let someone see, acquaint with”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ سَأَلَتْهُ عَنْ أَهْلِهِ وَعِيَالِهِ فَكَشَفَ لَهَا عَنْ جَمِيعِ أَحْوَالِهِ وَمَا هُوَ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: thumma saʾalathu ʿan ahlihi wa-ʿiyālihi fa-kashafa lahā ʿan jamīʿi aḥwālihi wa-mā huwa fīhi
sentences.l: Then she-asked-him about his-family and his-dependants, and he-uncovered to-her about all his-circumstances and what he (is) in-it.
sentences.i: Then she asked him about his family and household, and he laid open to her all his circumstances and the state he was in.
sentences.n: ahl, “family, people”, and ʿiyāl, “dependants”, those one supports, especially wife and children. kashafa ʿan, “to uncover, reveal”, ʿan marking what is laid bare. mā huwa fīhi, “what he is in”, i.e. his situation.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهَا إِنَّ لِي دَارٌ غَيْرُ هَذِهِ الدَّارِ جَعَلْتُهَا لِلِاجْتِمَاعِ بِالْأَصْحَابِ وَالْإِخْوَانِ وَلَيْسَ لِي فِيهَا أَحَدٌ إِلَّا الْجَارِيَةُ الَّتِي قُلْتُ عَلَيْهَا لِجَارِيَتِكِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahā inna lī dārun ghayru hādhihi al-dāri jaʿaltuhā li-al-ijtimāʿi bi-al-aṣḥābi wa-al-ikhwāni wa-laysa lī fīhā aḥadun illā al-jāriyatu allatī qultu ʿalayhā li-jāriyatiki
sentences.l: And he-said to-her: Indeed to-me (is) a house other-than this house, I-made-it for the meeting with the companions and the brothers; and there-is-not to-me in-it anyone except the slave-girl whom I-told about-her to-your-slave-girl.
sentences.i: And he said to her, “I have a house besides this one, which I keep for gatherings with my friends and brothers, and I have no one in it but the slave-woman I told your slave-girl about.”
sentences.n: inna lī dārun: after inna the noun should be accusative, dāran, written دارا; the print has no alif, so the word is read in the plain Middle Arabic way, without the case ending Classical would require, and ghayru agrees with it. jaʿala li-, “to set aside for”: li- gives the purpose. al-ijtimāʿ bi-, “meeting with”, bi- marking the people met. qultu ʿalayhā, “I spoke about her”, is the same qāla ʿalā as above.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ سَأَلَتْهُ عَنْ كَيْفِيَّةِ اطِّلَاعِهِ عَلَى أَصْلِ الْقِصَّةِ وَقِصَّةِ أَبِي الْحَسَنِ وَسَبَبِ سَفَرِهِ فَأَخْبَرَهَا بِمَاخَطَرَ بِبَالِهِ وَدَعَاهُ عَلَى السَّفَرِفَتَأَوَّهَتْ لِفِرَاقِ أَبِى الْحَسَنِ
sentences.tr: thumma saʾalathu ʿan kayfiyyati iṭṭilāʿihi ʿalā aṣli al-qiṣṣati wa-qiṣṣati Abī al-Ḥasani wa-sababi safarihi fa-akhbarahā bi-mā khaṭara bi-bālihi wa-daʿāhu ʿalā al-safari fa-taʾawwahat li-firāqi Abī al-Ḥasani
sentences.l: Then she-asked-him about the how of his-coming-to-know of the root of the story, and the story of Abū al-Ḥasan, and the cause of his-journey; and he-told-her of what had-come to his-mind and had-called-him to the journey; and she-sighed for the parting of Abū al-Ḥasan.
sentences.i: Then she asked him how he had come to learn how the affair began, and about Abū al-Ḥasan's story and why he had gone away; and he told her what had come into Abū al-Ḥasan's mind and driven him to travel. At that she sighed for the loss of Abū al-Ḥasan.
sentences.n: kayfiyya, “manner, how-ness”, an abstract noun from kayfa, “how?”. iṭṭalaʿa ʿalā (Form VIII), “to come to know of, be informed of”. akhbara bi-, “to tell of”, bi- marking what is told; the print runs bi-mā, “of what”, into the next word (بماخطر), and al-safar into fa-taʾawwahat (السفرفتاوّهت). khaṭara bi-bālihi, “it occurred to his mind”, and daʿāhu ʿalā al-safar, “called him to travel”: the likeliest reading makes Abū al-Ḥasan's own worry the subject of both, though bi-bālihi, “to his mind”, could also be the jeweller's; Classical would have daʿā ilā. taʾawwaha (Form V), “to sigh, say āh”; li- gives the cause. The print writes Abī both with ي and with ى (ابي, ابى) in this sentence.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ يَا فُلَانُ اعْلَمْ أَنَّ أَرْوَاحَ النَّاسِ مُتَلَائِمَةٌ فِى الشَّهَوَاتِ وَالنَّاسُ بِالنَّاسِ لَايَتِمُّ عَمَلٌ إِلَّا بِقَوْلٍ وَلَا يَتِمُّ غَرَضٌ إِلَّا بِسَعْيٍ وَلَاتَحْصُلُ رَاحَةٌ إِلَّا بَعْدَ تَعَبٍ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat yā fulānu iʿlam anna arwāḥa al-nāsi mutalāʾimatun fī al-shahawāti wa-al-nāsu bi-al-nāsi lā yatimmu ʿamalun illā bi-qawlin wa-lā yatimmu gharaḍun illā bi-saʿyin wa-lā taḥṣulu rāḥatun illā baʿda taʿabin
sentences.l: And she-said: O So-and-so, know that the spirits of people (are) in-accord in the desires, and people (are) by people: no deed is-completed except by a word, and no aim is-completed except by striving, and no rest comes-about except after toil.
sentences.i: And she said, “Know, my friend, that people's souls are drawn together by their desires, and people depend on people: no deed is done without a word, no aim is reached without effort, and no rest is had except after toil.”
sentences.n: The print has بصعي, a misprint for بسعي, corrected here. yā fulān, “O so-and-so”, stands in for the jeweller's name, which the story never gives. mutalāʾim (Form VI participle), “agreeing, suited to one another”; the hamza (ئ) is the print's own. al-nāsu bi-al-nāsi, “people are by people”, a saying: bi- here means “through, by means of”, people get on only with one another's help. The three clauses that follow are built alike, lā … illā, “no … except”; the print sets lāyatimmu and lātaḥṣulu as one word but lā yatimmu as two.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she ceased the speech allowed her.
